catalog_quote: Descriptively, we may say that in Michif words of three syllables or fewer, primary stress falls on the final syllable and secondary stress surfaces in three syllable words on the first syllable, while in words of four syllables or more, primary stress falls on the antepenult and secondary stress is alternating throughout the word. Note that this pattern holds regardless of the language source of the word in question: historically Cree (data in 1-5, a, b) and historically French (data in 1-3, c,d) lexical items, as well as items of mixed origin (data in 4c-d, 5c, 6a) pattern in the same way. ... First of all, Michif stress may be characterized as consisting of bounded iambs, from the right edge. ... in words of three syllables or less stress is word-final while in words of more than three syllables it is on the antepenult. ... sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title only: Rosen (2006) 'Language contact and Michif stress assignment', STUF 59(2):170-190, already in the per-language bibliography. It is squarely about Michif word stress but the full text is paywalled at De Gruyter (live page returns an AWS WAF challenge; Semantic Scholar marks it CLOSED; CORE, the Internet Archive PDF and academia/scholar lookups gave nothing; The abstract, recovered from a 2024 Internet Archive copy of the De Gruyter page and, says the paper offers a first analysis of Michif word stress, derives the system from both Plains Cree and French, and finds Cree- and French-source words pattern alike - consistent with the catalog's classification but without naming the stressed syllable. The catalog's deciding source, Rosen's 2007 Toronto dissertation (Chapter 7 'Michif Stress', p. 221), is held by the project and the PDF), cites the 2006 article, and gives the full statement (final primary stress in words of three syllables or fewer, antepenultimate in four or more, regardless of source); the 2006 article is the earlier journal version of that analysis, so acquiring it is low priority - it would at most refine, not replace, the dissertation. No new first-hand statement was read in this search of works with stress in the title; the catalog's 'fixed-unreviewed' entry with the Rosen 2007 quote stands.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: All three quote segments are verbatim: 'Descriptively, we may say that in Michif words of three syllables or fewer, primary stress falls on the final syllable.. regardless of the language source of the word in question' at printed p. 221 (PDF p. 234, checked with extracted text); '(12) Michif parameter settings: (i) bounded feet yes, binary (ii) Headedness R-headed (iambs) (iii) Directionality R-to-L (iv) Iterativity yes, iterative (v) Extrametricality Right-most foot is extrametrical' at p. 224 (PDF p. 237) - only differences are the flattened list layout and the dropped footnote marker '10' after 'settings:'; 'Note that word-final syllables are stressed even though they are extrametrical.…
new_statements.relation_note: This is the catalog's own deciding source (the Glottolog '2008' entry is the TWPL print of the 2007 dissertation, confirmed by the MPG PuRe metadata). Re-read from the PDF we hold: every catalog quote segment is verbatim at the stated pages, and the descriptive generalization (final for <=3 syllables, antepenult for >=4) matches the stress on syllable 2 of 2, 3 of 3, 2 of 4, 3 of 5, 4 of 6, 5 of 7, 6 of 8 (the 8-syllable grid is an extrapolation of 'four syllables or more', data run to 7 syllables). Sec. 7.4 adds the comparison: Michif patterns like French in 3-syllable words and like Plains Cree in 4+-syllable words, 'an amalgam of the two source language systems' (pp. 233-235).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Weight-insensitive, syllable-count rule at the phonological-word level: primary stress is word-final in words of one to three syllables and antepenultimate in words of four or more syllables, for Cree-, French- and mixed-source vocabulary alike. Formally: binary iambs built right-to-left, iteratively, with the rightmost foot extrametrical and main stress permitted only on a branching foot (hence final stress in 3-syllable words, where the leftmost foot is degenerate). Preverbs and other 'minor categories' (past ki+, want nohte+, future ka+) form their own stress domain, so syllables are counted only from the + boundary (p. 222).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of three-syllable words (p. 219); in words of four or more syllables secondary stress falls on alternating syllables in both directions from the primary, and the word-final syllable is always (secondarily) stressed even though its foot is extrametrical, attributed to phonetic final lengthening (pp. 220, 225).
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 10 p. 224: 'This stress system applies to most lexical items, but not always to a few invariable words such as tánde "when". There is further some deletion of unstressed [lax high vowel], rendering opaque some stress patterns.' Sec. 7.2.1.1 p. 223: compounds (incorporated nominal + 'be'/'make' verbs) stress the final syllable of the incorporated nominal instead of the antepenult, left unanalysed. Sec. 7.2.1 p. 222: apparent counter-examples with preverbs are resolved by the separate stress domain. Note Rosen's own slip on p. 221 ('a stress change from final to penultimate') where her data and formalization give antepenultimate.
new_statements.identity_note: Rosen 2007 describes the Manitoba dialect of Michif from three speakers (Norman Fleury; Grace Zoldy and Rita Flamand, from a different community), p. 9 (PDF p. 22); Glottolog languoid = Heritage Michif (mich1243), the Cree-French mixed language, correct match. The '2008' Glottolog citation and the catalog's '2007' dissertation are the same work (MPG PuRe item_406170: accepted 2007, in print in TWPL 2008).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among sources actually read: only Rosen 2007 was readable, and it agrees with the catalog record it underlies. The two unopened works cannot be compared. The catalog notes record a latent tension with Bakker's APiCS survey (which hedges between French final stress and Cree alternating stress and mentions dropped unstressed syllables) and with a Cree-keyed coding of 3-syllable words (Plains Cree antepenult vs Rosen's Michif final with initial secondary); Rosen herself addresses this by showing Michif is neither system but a syllable-count amalgam (pp. 233-235). Whether Bakker 1997 pp. 80-83 or Evans 1982 states anything different remains unverified.

sources.quote: This paper examines stress assignment in Michif, a contact language with its roots in French and Plains Cree ... First, to propose a first analysis of word stress in Michif, and second, to compare Michif word stress with Plains Cree and French word stress assignment systems ... I show that the Michif stress system derives from both the Plains Cree and French stress systems ... the new system is distinct from either, as lexical items from both Plains Cree and French vocabularies pattern in the same way. This is evidence against the commonly held view that Michif displays a split phonology based on language source (BAKKER 1997, BAKKER & PAPEN 1997, PAPEN 2003).
